rv.q: Director Jonathan Munby's sumptuously realised production successfully bridges the tonal shift
As with many of Miller’s better-known plays, it’s implacable: the past piles into the present and the action cannot stop until all the truths are out.
Even a lesser Miller is greater than most.
The results are astounding, this adaptation is as good as the play can be.
A superbly acted Arthur Miller masterclass in family tension, where the real price isn't on anything in the attic.

From sedate beginnings, Miller builds the simmering familial scene to an emotional crescendo which is frequently and humorously broken by the re-emergence from the bedroom, of the elderly and meddling Solomon who has his eyes on the prize and won’t be deterred.
And so he invites a furniture dealer, Henry Goodman’s Gregory Solomon, to assess and hopefully purchase all the properties.
The Price is not Miller's finest play, due to the sluggish middle section
The Price is possibly Miller's most philosophical endeavour, beautifully realised but in need of a gentle fine-tuning.

cn.t: Critics praise this compelling revival of Arthur Miller's 1967 drama for its superb ensemble performances, particularly Henry Goodman's standout turn, and the director's skill in highlighting the play's sharp humor amid its exploration of family tensions.
